content.intro: In this lesson, you will study algorithm correctness as part of Mathematical Foundations and Complexity Analysis. The attached PDF syllabus defines the topic coverage; the explanations and examples are original course material intended to help you reason through that coverage.
content.why_it_matters: Algorithm Correctness matters because DSA solutions need an explicit data representation, well-defined operations, and a defensible performance trade-off. Use the small example as a starting point, not as a substitute for testing your own implementation.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson focuses on algorithm correctness within Mathematical Foundations and Complexity Analysis. Start with the specific syllabus items rather than memorizing names: Preconditions and Postconditions; Loop Invariants; Proof by Induction; Proving Recursive Algorithms Correct; Counterexamples and Edge Cases. Identify the input, the supported operations, and the condition that makes the algorithm correct.

content_blocks.title: How the subtopics connect
content_blocks.text: The PDF lists the following concepts for this lesson: Preconditions and Postconditions; Loop Invariants; Proof by Induction; Proving Recursive Algorithms Correct; Counterexamples and Edge Cases. Treat these as connected parts of one problem-solving workflow. Define the state and assumptions, perform the operation, preserve the needed invariant, then inspect the output.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable Python example: Algorithm Correctness
content_blocks.code:
prices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]
best = 0
minimum = prices[0]
for price in prices[1:]:
    best = max(best, price - minimum)
    minimum = min(minimum, price)
print(best)

content_blocks.title: Correctness checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Greedy reasoning keeps a compact summary of past choices; a proof must justify why discarded information cannot improve the answer. Before relying on the result, state your preconditions, identify the invariant or key argument, and test an input that violates a common assumption.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Implement or trace a small example of algorithm correctness. First write one normal input and its expected result, then add a boundary case. Explain why the result is correct and analyze time and auxiliary space.

common_mistakes.why: A normal case may hide empty-input, duplicate-value, ordering, disconnected-input or off-by-one errors.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, boundary and invalid cases and state which inputs the implementation supports.

common_mistakes.problem: Guessing complexity from the code length.
common_mistakes.why: Loops, nested work, recursion, data structure operations and input properties determine the cost.
common_mistakes.fix: Count dominant operations as a function of input size and distinguish auxiliary memory from input storage.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a code snippet as a complete production implementation.
common_mistakes.why: A teaching example often omits input validation, robust tests or special cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the linked exercise and local tests to extend it; record runtime assumptions and limitations.
